prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength principle, and for its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 through control of the systematic shifts

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B013 as my single preferred part. The chair asks whether the lattice clock is a discovery or a measurement advance. My answer is that the magic-wavelength condition is a discovery in the atomic-physics sense: a specific, nonobvious statement that for a chosen wavelength the differential light shift between the two clock levels vanishes to first order, so that a trapping potential does not disturb the transition it is meant to hold. That idea has a named originator (Katori). The 10^-18 result then shows that the idea survives contact with blackbody radiation, density shifts, tunnelling and higher-order lattice shifts, which was far from guaranteed, and that is the part associated with Ye's group. Both halves are measured, independently reproduced with several species in several laboratories, and used: clock-to-clock comparisons now resolve the gravitational redshift over centimetre height differences and set limits on drifts of fundamental constants. On timing, I side with Kroll that a pending redefinition of the second is evidence of maturity and not a reason to wait, because the redefinition depends on exactly the clock performance this prize would recognise. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, shared by every proposal that ranks the candidate. No other ballot offers a citation that names a precise concept and a precise demonstrated number.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that this reads as precision metrology and not as a new phenomenon, and that the prize would sit beside the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-quantum-system control. I think the clock is distinct from both, since neither the comb nor ion trapping contains the lattice magic-wavelength principle, but I accept that a committee which wants a discovery of new physics could rank B041 or B001 higher. Other strontium, ytterbium and mercury lattice groups and the single-ion clock community are outside a two-name credit, and some early lattice-clock work by other groups is a fair complaint. I also have to concede to Mehlig and Johansson that B001 and B041 reach further into neighbouring fields. Finally, B013 has no more than two explicit supporters, so I cannot claim a majority for it.

responses.point: Kroll moved to B013 from B003, argues that a pending redefinition of the second is evidence of maturity, and wants Yb and Hg lattice clocks and cross-laboratory Sr/Yb comparisons to count as maturity evidence and not as credited names.
responses.response: I accept both points and have adopted them. The redefinition argument is correct, because the case for redefining the second rests on the same 10^-18 performance a prize would recognise, so it measures maturity and does not call for waiting. I also accept the species point: Yb, Hg and cross-species comparisons are why I regard the idea as robust, and they do not need to be credited names. I have changed my citation to follow your structure, concept first and realisation second. One place I would still press you is that the citation should say 'optical lattice clock' without restricting it to strontium, so that it does not read as a prize for one atom. Where we both remain exposed is the chair's question about whether this is a discovery. I do not think we should claim more than the evidence supports: it is an invention that was then demonstrated at the limit, and we should say so.

responses.point: Johansson rates B013 fifth only because of timing, argues that the Academy might want the redefinition of the second to come first, and judges the clock narrower in reach than B001 while agreeing the credit is better defined.
responses.response: On timing I disagree. The redefinition is an international metrology decision that depends on a roadmap of clock comparisons and on the clocks working as claimed; waiting for it would make a prize for the performance conditional on a bureaucratic process that the performance itself drives. On reach, I accept that B001 connects more fields, but the lattice clock reaches relativistic geodesy, tests of constant variation and searches for dark-matter-induced oscillations, so I would call it deep and not narrow. I also welcome your movement to a mixed B001 prize with Zoller. It resolves part of my earlier hesitation by naming the proposal along with the experiments. I still do not see how the B001 citation avoids leaving out Esslinger or Jaksch, and I would not want the committee to choose it merely because it can be assembled from five names. If B001 is chosen after all, your Bloch, Greiner and Zoller trio is a more defensible structure than a pure experiment-only trio, though I notice that this takes a position on credit that Mehlig does not share.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 as an experiment-only prize (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) for the controllable Hubbard-model laboratory, acknowledging that quantum simulation has so far reproduced known physics more than it has solved an open problem.
responses.response: I agree with your own caveat, and it is the main reason I still hold B001 as an alternative and not as my first choice. If the claim is that these experiments gave quantitative access to problems that are intractable otherwise, the committee needs at least one clear case where the simulator answered a question that theory could not, and the fermionic Hubbard results at low temperature are not there yet. By comparison, the lattice clock delivers a measured number that nothing else in the field matches. I also think your experiment-only trio and Johansson's mixed trio are two different prizes, and the committee should choose which one it means before counting 'B001 support' as one bloc. I would be content with your experimental trio if the committee prefers B001, and I would then ask that the citation avoid the phrase 'quantum simulation' as a finished achievement.

responses.point: Eriksson judges B041 a compact theory prediction followed by experiment, but accepts that the unresolved pairing mechanism, sample dependence and the omission of the first-author experimentalists argue for waiting.
responses.response: I find the sequence prediction then observation persuasive, and it is a stronger structure than the Higgs credit. Your own reservations, together with Danielsson's and Mehlig's on the pairing mechanism, are the reasons I keep B041 second to B013 for now: the interpretation is still moving. I would put the question to you and Olsson differently from the chair. The flat-band prediction and the finding of correlated insulating states do not depend on the superconductivity mechanism, so the discovery could be credited without claiming the mechanism. If the citation is limited to that, I find the maturity objection weaker than I did. The remaining concern, the omission of Cao and Dean, I cannot resolve for you, and I would not want a citation that implies the group leader made the discovery alone.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery (B020), crediting the conception and leadership of ATLAS and CMS to Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, and says the attribution problem is not resolved.
responses.response: I do not dispute that the Higgs observation is unrecognised on the experimental side or that it is mature. My difficulty is the one you state. The chair asks for a rule that selects three of four names. Leadership at conception (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) and leadership at announcement (Gianotti) lead to different trios, and the committee would be choosing a rule as much as a discovery. I do not see a rule that is convincing without relying on judgement about who led, which is not what the prize language asks for. I would reconsider B020 if the committee could write a citation naming both experiments for a defined contribution to the discovery, not for a role. Without that, I rank it behind the three candidates that have an identifiable intellectual contribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as an invention plus demonstration (my view) or as a measurement advance that falls short of the discovery standard.

Whether the citation should be limited to the strontium and ytterbium alkaline-earth lattice clocks or phrased for optical lattice clocks in general, and whether two names are sufficient given contemporaneous work by other groups.
Whether B001 can be given a defensible three-name form, and if so whether the committee would choose the experimental or the mixed structure.
How much of the B041 maturity objection remains if the citation avoids the superconducting mechanism, which I am not qualified to judge.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my documented profile. I have long-running collaborations in attosecond physics with L'Huillier and the Lund group, with Keller's group at ETH, and with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom is a credited name on B013, B041 or B020. B001 credits Bloch, Esslinger, Greiner, Zoller and Cirac; I have no documented collaboration with them, and I would update this note if the committee turned to a candidate where a collaborator is credited.
